lines.text:
A Room for Everyone

The living room is the heart of our home. It is where the whole family comes together in the evening to relax, chat, and spend time with each other.

In the centre of the room, there is a large sofa and two armchairs arranged around a coffee table. My father usually sits in the rocking chair by the window and reads the newspaper. My younger brother prefers the ottoman — he uses it as a seat while he plays on the game console connected to the television.

We have a tall bookshelf against the wall, filled with books, photo frames, and a small plant in a vase. Next to it is the TV stand with a sound bar and the Wi-Fi router tucked behind it. All the cables go into a power strip hidden behind the cabinet.

The room feels warm because of the details. There is a soft rug on the floor, cushions on the sofa, and a throw blanket draped over the armchair. My mother hung curtains that match the colour of the walls, and she placed a few candles in candle holders on the side table.

For lighting, we have a ceiling light for bright evenings and a floor lamp in the corner for softer light when we watch TV. String lights decorate the shelf during holidays.

On weekends, we sometimes play board games or put together a puzzle on the dining table. Other times, we just sit down, listen to music through the speaker, and take a nap. The living room is not the biggest room, but it is definitely the most loved.

lines.text: Living Room vs Lounge vs Den
lines.name: Living Room vs Lounge vs Den

lines.text: 'Living room' is the most common term. 'Lounge' is British and slightly formal. 'Den' (American) is a smaller, cosier room for relaxing. 'Family room' emphasises casual family use.
lines.name: 'Living room' is the most common term. 'Lounge' is British and slightly formal. 'Den' (American) is a smaller, cosier room for relaxing. 'Family room' emphasises casual family use.

lines.text: 'Furniture' is uncountable in English. Say 'a piece of furniture' or 'some furniture' — never 'a furniture' or 'furnitures'. Same rule applies to 'equipment' and 'luggage'.

lines.text: In many English-speaking homes, guests may keep shoes on unless told otherwise. In contrast, many cultures expect shoes off. A doormat at the entrance is a common feature — some homes provide slippers.

lines.text: Complimenting someone's living room is good small talk: 'What a lovely room!', 'I love your sofa!', 'This is such a cosy space.' It's polite and shows interest in the host's home.
